content_html:
Edit a language model inside a range, and let anyone check, byte for byte, what changed and what did not.

Fine-tuning, LoRA, merging and quantization can move the output at any position. After such an edit, the only way to know that "nothing else changed" is to evaluate everything again, and even then you only know it for the prompts you tried. In our runs on Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3-8B, a 4-bit quantization and a public fine-tuned derivative each left 0 of 150 greedy answers the same as the original's.

Kestrom takes the other side. Each edit comes with a range that is read from the weights or from the decoding, not from what the editor claims, and a report that anyone can rebuild on their own machine and compare with cmp.

original weights ──edit──▶ edited weights ──kestrom-verify──▶ report.json
                                                   │  W   every byte the same but the changed rows
                                                   │  U0  the original equal to itself on this machine
                                                   │  G1  every logit outside the range equal, bit for bit (row edits)
                                                   │  G2  greedy output the same until the range is reached
                                                   ▼
                                  the receiver rebuilds report.json ─▶ same bytes

Two packages:

Package Command What it is License
kestrom-verify kestrom-verify The checker. Reads two models (and their outputs) and writes the report Apache-2.0, free for everyone
kestrom kestrom The editing tools whose range the checker can bound Free for companies with fewer than 100 people, for noncommercial use and for a trial of less than 32 days (PolyForm); other uses need a commercial license

Three tiers of guarantee

The checks that pass say which tier an edit is in. Kestrom does not blur them.

Tier What is checked Commands Edits
1. Outputs Greedy output is the same until the range is reached (G2); for a row edit, every logit outside the range is also bit-identical to the original (G1). With an output layer tied to the embedding, both for inputs with no changed id Row edits: range, logits, compare. Decode-time edits: compare events kestrom rows (rows of the output layer), kestrom generate (decode-time edits: rules—including probed models fitted at a decoder layer and transferred via kestrom bridge rules, conditional steering including directions/conditions mapped via kestrom bridge, adding a direction after a given text, phrase bans, loop stopping, open lines, compiled fact-KV routing via kestrom kv compile + kv: lines), kestrom ifc (twin-track control-flow non-interference and secret leakage firewall)
2. Weights Only the declared tensors / rows changed (declaration check D). How much the outputs moved is counted, not bounded diff, measure kestrom edit (neuron and head gains, a head's write along a direction, keyed writes, neuron writes, a direction out of a few down_proj columns), kestrom rules write-mlp (rules in MLP neurons), kestrom trigger (spare rows of the embedding)
3. Measured only What changed, and how much measure, diff kestrom merge, and any fine-tune (LoRA too) or quantization made elsewhere

Determinism (U0: the original model gives the same logits and the same greedy output twice on your machine) is checked by logits and measure, which run the original twice, and by compare, on the two outputs of the original you give it. If U0 fails, G1 and G2 in that report mean nothing. range and diff read only bytes. compare checks the output files you give it: write them yourself, running the original twice. For decode-time edits it checks the output against the events the decoding records, not that a loop or a condition was really there.

The editing tools

Product scope:

  • Supported (enterprise evaluation / audit): kestrom-verify (Apache-2.0), kestrom audit, kestrom inspect (including mirror and disarm), kestrom ifc (control / firewall), kestrom kv + kestrom generate --rules (open, loopguard, phrase, add, ban), kestrom rules (fit, run, build, weigh), kestrom steer, kestrom rows ban-row / ban, and kestrom bridge.
  • Experimental (research / reproduction): kestrom edit, kestrom trigger, kestrom find, kestrom rows lsq / ftpo, kestrom rules write-mlp, kestrom train sft-data, and kestrom merge.

Every tool is in, whether or not it reached the target we set for it. The table gives the tier and what we measured, with the target where one was missed. A tool's guarantee says what did not change; whether the edit does what you want is measured, and for several tools it fell short. Each command's help (kestrom, kestrom <command> --help, python -m pydoc kestrom.<module>) has the details.

kestrom generate --rules: a loopguard line Goes back at a thinking loop and forbids repeated 16-token pieces 1 Correct 4 → 26 of 100 (Qwen3.5-0.8B; below)
kestrom generate --rules: an open line The output opens with the class that rules of their own (kestrom rules run, no model) answer for the prompt's data, then a line feed: the top token is kept where the text still fits, else the top token that fits is taken (an event); where the rules answer none, nothing, or a class given in the line. The answer is what follows the last </think>; where the top token that begins it starts no class of the head nor the class given in the line, nothing. With a text in the line, the thinking also opens with that text, the class in it 1 Qwen3.5-4B writing a class on line 1 and a reason on line 2, opened by agent-written rules that route Japanese questions about building energy (the rules of kestrom rules run below): on 24 new questions (8 plain, 8 oddly worded, 8 vague or unrelated; written by one agent, kept where a second gave the same answer) line 1 was right on 13 unopened, 15 opened with the rules' class, 22 when also opened with clarify where the rules answer none; no line 1 went from right to wrong; G2 24/24 in both forms. One question the rules could not read (a typo) was opened with clarify though it had an answer; the model alone was wrong there too, and how often it would have been right is not measured. In a run of the same method by an earlier script, one judging agent found the reason newly contradicting line 1 or misreading the question on 1 of the 24. Four chat questions with no request for a class (two naming a word the example router reads) kept the original's output, token for token (the example). With thinking on and at most 2,048 tokens, on the same 24 questions: line 1 right on 4 unopened (19 outputs never closed the thinking), 4 with the answer opened (every output the original's), 11 with one sentence holding the rules' class (clarify where they answer none) also written at the start of the thinking (8 that had not closed the thinking became right, 1 that was right no longer closed it; 13 never closed the thinking, and none more did with a loop guard of 512); G2 24/24 in each form, where it covers little of an output whose thinking was opened. All three counts are below those of the same questions with thinking off (13 unopened, 22 opened with clarify where the rules answer none); of those 8, 6 are questions the unopened model has right with thinking off and 2 are ones it has wrong. One wording of the sentence; the unopened model at a higher limit is not measured. One model; the agents that wrote the rules and the questions, labelled and judged are of one family. examples/rules-open runs the mechanism on eight other questions
kestrom kv compile, kestrom kv chat, kestrom generate --rules: a kv line Compiles per-fact system-prefix KV caches from standalone rules and FACTS.json (zero weights changed); at decode time (kv: BANK_DIR [MAX_MATCH]), evaluates the bank's rules on data plus any in NAME: prompt FILE LAYER conditions (including cross-model probes mapped by kestrom bridge map) passed as 0/1 values, injects the compiled KV cache when 1 to MAX_MATCH entries match (composing ≥2 on demand with an in-memory LRU cache) and records event 0, while unmatched or out-of-range prompts get no cache and no event (events=[] where no other line acts). kestrom kv chat runs multi-turn sessions (steps/prev + optional PROBES.dsl) with incremental KV reuse when the topic holds and automatic re-prefill or rebuild on switches (tier 1 here is for kestrom generate with a kv line) 1 Gemma 4 E4B on 149 fresh unseen Japanese building-fact questions across 27 cells (9 floors × 3 categories, scored by 4 blind readers, research script): 132/149 raw right (130/149 with answer check), 4 wrong, vs 89/149 with no knowledge text and 137/149 with the matching fact in the prompt; recompiling 6 edited cells took 0.19s (0.95s for all 27) with all 21 unedited KV caches bit-identical (~976.9 KB/fact). Multi-domain composed kv: BANK 2 + 5-turn kestrom kv chat (stateful prev DSL, 2 domains): on Gemma 4 E4B, 4/4 U0/G2 PASS (cmp identical; composed prompt recalled both keys) and 5/5 chat turns accurate (plain → switch → incremental reuse on follow-up pronoun with 25-token delta prefill → compose recalling both → switch); on Qwen3.5-0.8B (mlx_lm 0.31.1), 5/5 chat turns accurate with automatic rebuild on history re-tokenization and ArraysCache composition. Hybrid regex + bridged prompt-probe routing (Qwen3.5-4B → Gemma 4 E4B layer 22 mapped by kestrom bridge map, 2-entry bank, mean_kb 2,028.6 KB, 22 held-out prompts = 10 science + 10 Python + 2 鉄壁の結界): with disjoint phrasing-matched unlabeled CALIB_PROMPTS (threshold=-7.8604), 10/10 science got kv="science" (events=[0], all 10 replied in Japanese with the cassette tag), 2/2 鉄壁の結界 got kv="barrier", 10/10 Python were bit-identical (kv=null, events=[]), and U0/G2 22/22 PASS (cmp identical), plus 3-turn kestrom kv chat ... PROBES.dsl went plain (p_sci=0, Python) → switch (p_sci=1, kv="science") → reuse (p_sci=0 follow-up carried by prev, 17-token delta prefill); phrasing-mismatched CALIB_PROMPTS (threshold=-6.1144) triggered only 2/10 science while keeping 10/10 Python bit-identical and U0/G2 22/22 PASS. Mechanism is cached system-turn KV context, not a weight edit; G2 covers nothing after position 0 on matched prompts
kestrom trigger Spare rows of the embedding, learned as a trigger 2 With the trigger, polite sentences 0.641 → 0.017; without it, every logit of 150 prompts equal. JMMLU with the trigger 0.74 → 0.71, target ≤ 1 point not reached (Qwen3.5-9B)
kestrom generate --rules: add lines with in … after, thinking or position One layer's output plus a direction, from the token that completes a given text, while thinking, or before given output positions 1 Not measured
kestrom generate --rules: ban lines Logits of tokens set to −inf where a unit fires 1 Not measured. A ban is of tokens, not characters: banning 、 left the token 、「 free (Qwen3.5-0.8B); to keep a string out, use a phrase line
kestrom ifc control Twin-track greedy decoding separating JSON CONTROL keys (from clean Track B, untrusted data masked) and DATA keys (from full Track A, clamping single tokens that cross back into control syntax). fast (default) switches tracks lazily so only one track runs per token; audit runs both tracks every step and logs every control_override. Runs on mlx (default) or torch (CUDA, MPS, CPU) 1 40 realistic JSON tool-calling prompts (10 benign, 30 prompt injections; system prompt lists available tools, MLX): on Qwen3.5-0.8B, control hijacks 23/30 → 0/30 (benign control 9/10 → 10/10, summary hits 10/10 benign and 27/30 inject; wall-clock time fast 1.43× vs audit 1.91× over unprotected base); on Qwen3.5-4B, control hijacks 12/30 → 0/30 (benign 10/10 with 0 overrides, summary hits 10/10 benign and 28/30 inject; wall-clock time fast 1.09× [50.1s vs 45.9s] vs audit 1.66× [76.4s]); U0 40/40 and G2 40/40 PASS on both models and both modes via unmodified kestrom-verify compare events (reports rebuilt byte for byte). On Linux + NVIDIA L4 CUDA (torch 2.14.1+cu130, transformers 5.22.1, default non-forced CUDA, Qwen3.5-4B, examples/ifc-control 3 prompts): hijacks 2/2 → 0/2, U0 3/3 and G2 3/3 PASS for both fast (20.4s vs base 22.9s) and audit (27.2s) with byte-identical reports (cmp); on macOS MPS (Qwen3.5-0.8B): U0 3/3 and G2 3/3 PASS. On 4 earlier JSON-escape smuggling prompts (Qwen3.5-4B, MLX) the base model was not fooled, so the boundary clamp did not fire on the model (tested in unit tests)
kestrom ifc firewall Twin-track greedy decoding against secret leakage: strict-public emits Track B (secret removed) with events=[]; gated-public emits Track A unless a token's log-probability lift over Track B reaches TAU (default 2.0 nats), then falls back to Track B. Runs on mlx (default) or torch (CUDA, MPS, CPU) 1 24 public+secret writing prompts (TAU=2.0, no keyword lists, MLX): on Qwen3.5-0.8B, unprotected Track A leaked on 21/24 (20 literal, 21 semantic) → strict-public 0/24 (24/24 bit-identical to secret-free Track B) and gated-public 0/24 (111 blocks; U0/G2 24/24 PASS; manual reading found repetition and echoed section headings on some 0.8B outputs); on Qwen3.5-4B, leaks 2/24 → strict-public 0/24 (24/24 bit-identical) and gated-public 0/24 (31 blocks; U0/G2 24/24 PASS); all reports rebuilt byte for byte. On Linux + NVIDIA L4 CUDA (torch, Qwen3.5-4B, 3 prompts): strict-public 3/3 bit-identical to Track B (U0/G2 3/3 PASS) and gated-public U0/G2 3/3 PASS with 0/3 leaks. strict-public follows Track B from token 0, so audit leak attempts on gated-public

kestrom edit neuron-gain An MLP neuron's activation times k (its up_proj row) 2 Not measured
kestrom edit head-gain An attention head's output times k (its columns of o_proj, or out_proj for linear attention) 2 Not measured
kestrom edit head-proj What a head writes along a direction, removed, flipped or amplified (CHiPS) 2 Not measured
kestrom edit keyed A rank-1 write into down_proj that a key opens at the positions to write and keeps shut on the others 2 32 relations written one by one: held-out question 32/32, one-hop use 31–32/32 in the training context; another person's fact in the prompt kept 31/32 once DATA also left the question's name slot filled by unused names (24–26/32 with the other settings); outside answers 223–234/240 the same; in 64 unseen contexts (second set rebuilt, report only), 40/64 org and 32/64 city despite κ·x 0.96 and 63–64/64 stated facts (Qwen3.5-9B; below)
kestrom edit neuron-write The least-used neurons rewritten to write a direction where a key opens (one neuron, or a capped pair) 2 Not measured
kestrom rules write-mlp The rules written into neurons of the last MLP 2 0.749–0.785 of sentences on target, target 0.835 not reached (PLaMo 3 Translate, earlier PyTorch form)
kestrom rules run, kestrom rules build, kestrom rules weigh Nothing: the rules run as a network of their own, with no model, on given texts (regexes: found, counted, or a number read) and values, once or step by step with the units of the step before as inputs (prev lines) and numbers kept in registers (set lines), scored against labels and numeric targets; build writes that network out, and weigh fits the coefficients of the out lines to labels by least squares, the other lines kept as written — A hand-written router of Japanese questions about building energy (88 regexes, two layers of 17 units; intent and floor), rewritten as rules by a script, the questions normalized as the original does before run reads them: over 322 questions and both heads, of the 632 answers where fewer than two classes fired, run gave the original's class in 514, and no answer in the other 118, where the original gave its default (ask back, no floor), counted as the same. Where two floors fired (12), the original answered the one first in its list of classes and run gives no answer. Rules for the same task written by an agent from 322 labelled questions and a description of the task (85 lines: 25 match inputs, 43 units, two heads; written out by a short script of its own, tried on six questions of its own, and the first version it scored): of 60 new questions, written afterwards by a second agent from the description alone and given the same answers by a third, 55 right, 4 no answer, 1 wrong (fixed before the run: at least 0.70 right, at most 0.05 wrong). The three agents are one model family and the questions are not from users. The count, number, prev and set lines, more than 32 units and weigh: not measured
kestrom train sft-data Fine-tuning data (prompt-completion pairs) from the edited outputs 3 A LoRA trained on it with mlx_lm: listed phrases −99%, but it also copied its training answers; JMMLU 0.70 against 0.74 (Qwen3.5-9B)
kestrom merge A + λ (B − C), tensor by tensor 3 Qwen3.5-9B toward its Base at λ 0.25 and 0.5: listed phrases 3,527 and 3,716 against 3,092, no reduction
kestrom inspect, kestrom audit Nothing: reads a fine-tune delivered to you against what it declares (LoRA rank and targets, quantization, training data) and shows what the declaration does not explain, for you to judge: a quantization other than declared, tensors changed beyond the declared rank, what a change makes the model say (lens), tokens raised against fine-tunes you retrain from the declaration (behavior, against the mean of several), and the words that raise a token (trigger); a model received as a GGUF file is read back with the original quantized alike (gguf). For quantization-conditioned backdoors (dormant in FP16/BF16, active after quantization), mirror inspects a single checkpoint with no original model and no trigger prompts (spectral sign-coherence $\rho_1$ of $Q(W)-W$, cell-boundary clustering, active block collapse, and optional behavior-space comparison against $W_{\text{mirror}} = 2W - Q(W)$ and sign-randomized nulls), and disarm neutralizes only the flagged tensors with anchor-preserving stochastic rounding ($\mathbb{E}[Q_{\text{SR}}(W)] = W$ for values inside the quantizer grid). kestrom audit bundles optional diff (BASE_DIR + DECLARED.json) and mirror into deterministic audit.json, audit.html, and audit.sarif outputs 3 Models with known backdoors (Qwen3.5-0.8B): a two-neuron write in layer 7 stood out as one component (singular value 139, the LoRA's at most 0.28) that raised 芒果 and mango; the words raising rabbit for a write in layer 11 were wind, winds (z 15) and 气温, 风吹, 春风 (z 22–25), its trigger's topic. A blind test of 10 fine-tunes, 5 with a backdoor made by someone who did not know how inspect reads, judged by a model given only the outputs, the declarations and the command help: all 5 targets named, and 1 of the 5 clean models called backdoored (at confidence 0.45); a second such reader got all 10 right. The two readers named the trigger's words for 1 and 2 of the 5. A second blind test of 12, 4 with a backdoor, the model compared with the mean of three retrained references: both readers right on all 12, all 4 targets named, the trigger's words for 2 of the 4. The same 12 with the weights only (no declaration, data or references; compared with the original): both readers right on all 12, all 4 targets named. The same 12 as Q4_K_M GGUF files, weights only: both readers right on the 8 clean models and on 3 of the 4 backdoors with their targets; the missed one had the smallest behavior S of the 4 in the weights-only run, on a model quantized twice. Self-controlled mirror and disarm on MLX affine 4-bit (group 64, Qwen3.5-0.8B, plus weight scan on Qwen3.5-4B): zero false positives across official 0.8B/4B, an abliterated 0.8B derivative and a 16-tensor benign fine-tune (max $\rho_1$ 1.0165–1.0243, max b85 0.1562, behavior coherence 0.92–1.00×); across four box-PGD quantization-conditioned backdoors (16-tensor, 2-tensor conditional stealth, and two 6-tensor adaptive margin/histogram-matched attacks with b85 0.1495–0.1499 matching benign), mirror localized all 30/30 modified tensors with 0/900 false positives ($\rho_1$ 4.91–16.74), extracted the exact target token on trigger-free plain text (coherence 12.3–93.5×), and disarm cut 4-bit attack activation from 24/24 to 0/24 (1/24 on the histogram-matched model, matching BF16) while surviving subsequent standard 4-bit quantization; an outlier-injection block-collapse test was missed by $\rho_1$ and b85 and caught by block collapse (ge90 64–65 vs benign max 12). Extending mirror and disarm to PyTorch and 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4, group 64) on Linux + NVIDIA L4 CUDA (bitsandbytes 0.50.2) matched CUDA bitsandbytes FP32 NF4 dequantization exactly (max_abs_diff = 0.0), gave zero false positives and byte-exact reports on benign Qwen3.5-0.8B (186 tensors, max $\rho_1$ 1.0185, max b85 0.1583, behavior coherence 0.81×) and Qwen3.5-4B (248 tensors, max $\rho_1$ 1.0213, max b85 0.1509, behavior coherence 0.88×), and on a 2-tensor NF4 box-PGD backdoor localized all 2/2 modified tensors with 0/184 false positives (behavior coherence 3.84×) while disarm cut the real bitsandbytes 4-bit NF4 target-token logit jump from +9.60 to +0.87 with zero changed kestrom-verify diff output rows. The decode-time edits are all written in one rules language (python -m pydoc kestrom.rules) and combine freely. For example, plain style for free-form questions only, no Chinese tokens in the answer after thinking, no **, and the loop guard:

in free: prompt style.npz 16        # a condition read on the prompt (kestrom steer direction)
in think: thinking
h1 f: all(free)
h1 answer: all(!think)
h2 plain: all(f)
h2 ans: all(answer)
add style.npz 16: 14.6*plain        # conditional steering
ban 的 了 们: ans                    # these tokens never, once thinking is over
phrase: "**"                        # go back and avoid it
loopguard: 512

kestrom generate MODEL prompts.json out.jsonl --rules edit.dsl records the events of every line, and kestrom-verify compare events checks that each output is the original's until its first event. Rules that read probed features of the hidden state are fitted first (kestrom rules fit, optionally at a decoder LAYER >= 0 so kestrom bridge rules can transfer FIT.npz across models).

An open line connects rules written with no model to a model's answer: open meter: router.dsl ask runs the rules of router.dsl (a network of their own, below) on each prompt's data and makes the output open with the class their head meter answers and a line feed, or with ask where they answer none (without the last word, nothing is done there). Where the model's own top tokens already spell that class nothing is changed and no event is recorded; the first token replaced is an event, and what follows is the model's own continuation of the opening it was given. The answer is what follows the last </think>, and nothing is done while the model thinks. The line acts only where the model begins the answer with a class: where the top token that begins it starts none of the head's classes nor the class given in the line, the answer is left alone, as were four chat questions sent through the same rules. An answer that begins with the first characters of a class is opened whatever was asked, and a class written later in the answer is not touched. With a text as the last word (open meter: router.dsl ask "The rules have decided line 1: {}."), the thinking of a model that thinks also opens with that text, {} in it the class, and a line feed, so that the model thinks with the rules' answer before it. That text is written wherever thinking begins (with another token than </think>) and the rules answer or the line gives a class, so nearly every such output has an event at its first position and the check covers almost nothing of it; what the model thinks after the text is its own, and it may not stop. kestrom-verify compare events checks the output up to the first event; that the opening is the rules' class is read from OUT (open, data and the text), and whether the reason after it is true is not checked.

A kv line (kv: BANK_DIR [MAX_MATCH]) connects standalone rules directly to compiled per-fact prefix KV caches (kestrom kv compile MODEL RULES.dsl FACTS.json OUT_DIR [PREV_DIR]). Each fact in FACTS.json is prefilled offline once as a system-turn prefix of MODEL into its own .safetensors cache file, and PREV_DIR copies unchanged entries without recomputing so editing one subset of facts leaves unrelated caches bit-identical. At decode time, kestrom generate --rules evaluates any in NAME: prompt FILE LAYER conditions (including cross-model probes mapped by kestrom bridge map) on the raw prompt before decoding and passes their 0/1 results into data["values"] alongside each prompt's data (with "steps", into the last step's: earlier steps give their own; values given in data win; allowing "data" to be omitted when the bank reads only those prompt inputs): when an entry uniquely matches (or 2..MAX_MATCH match when MAX_MATCH > 1, composed and prefilled once via an in-memory LRU cache), only the prompt tokens after the shared prefix (with zero knowledge text in the prompt) are decoded on top of that cache, recording event 0 and "kv": KEY (a list when composed); when no entry matches (or more than MAX_MATCH match), no cache is injected and the kv line records no event ("kv": null); where no other line of the rules acts, events=[] and the output is bit-identical to the unchanged model. Because event 0 marks the start of a matched prompt, kestrom-verify compare events checks unmatched prompts up to the first event of another line and covers nothing after position 0 on matched ones. For multi-turn conversations, kestrom kv chat (MODEL BANK_DIR [MAX_TOKENS] [MAX_MATCH] [TURNS.json] [OUT.jsonl] [PROBES.dsl]) evaluates optional PROBES.dsl in ... prompt conditions on each raw turn together with the cumulative steps history through the bank's prev rules, reuses the live KV cache incrementally while the active keys stay unchanged and the chat template remains a strict prefix extension, and swaps/composes/re-prefills only when topics change or history tokens shift. Both kestrom generate and kestrom kv chat refuse a bank whose rules.dsl or cache files are not the ones its manifest.json hashed, or whose model fingerprint differs; the mechanism requires a chat template that places the system turn as a clean prefix before the user turn.

kestrom rules run RULES.dsl DATA.json OUT.jsonl runs rules of in, h1, h2, out and set lines as a network of their own, with no model: match, count and number lines read each entry's text by a regex, the other inputs are values given in DATA, and the out lines name classes. A layer may have any number of units. An entry may be a list of steps: the network runs once per step and in NAME: prev UNIT reads whether a unit fired at the step before, so the rules can keep a state (a parity, a mode, what was seen). A set REGISTER: a % b if UNIT line keeps a number along the steps and rewrites it where a unit fires, computed with + - * / // % (a counter, Euclid's algorithm); after one step it is a numeric output, scored against targets. Classes named HEAD/CLASS are answered per head. kestrom rules weigh RULES.dsl DATA.json OUT.dsl rewrites the out lines with coefficients fitted to the labels. run prints how many answers agree with the labels. Use it to try rules on inputs you choose, or to write a small classifier by hand. It edits nothing, so it has no tier; where a rule can be written as plain code, plain code does the same job.

To find where to edit, kestrom find reads the model and changes nothing: direction (the difference of two behaviours per layer, with Cohen's d on held-out answers), lens (what each MLP neuron writes into the vocabulary, or the neurons that write given words), reverse (neurons whose down_proj column points along the difference), writers (neurons by what they actually write along a direction) and heads (heads by how much zeroing each one lowers a direction). These and the edit commands rest on known methods (below) and add the declaration of the rows each edit wrote; each command's help says the choices we made.

Not included: orthogonalizing a direction out of every matrix that writes the residual (it removes refusals, which we do not provide a tool for; on a style direction it broke Qwen3.5-9B, JMMLU 0.74 → 0.16).

"Earlier PyTorch form": the numbers come from the research code on PLaMo 3 Translate; the Kestrom command is its MLX port, checked to run and to change only what it declares on Qwen3.5, not rerun for its effect. "Not measured": checked the same way, effect not measured.

Technical write-ups

  • Stop prompt injection and secret leaks by construction, then prove it byte for byte: kestrom ifc
  • Detect and disarm quantization-triggered LLM backdoors with no base model and no trigger: kestrom inspect mirror
  • Zero-regression KV hot-patching and zero-shot cross-model control transfer: kestrom kv and kestrom bridge
  • Questions & evaluation discussions: GitHub Discussions

What Kestrom does not guarantee

  • That the range is right: whether a banned token should be banned, whether a condition fires on the right prompts.
  • Agreement across runtimes. llama.cpp and MLX give different greedy outputs even for the same original weights. Compare the original and the edited model in the same runtime.
  • Sampling. The guarantees are about teacher-forced logits and greedy decoding.
  • Anything on the outputs for tier 2 and 3 edits: there the report only counts.
  • That a fine-tune has no backdoor. kestrom inspect shows evidence to read; nothing found does not mean nothing is there. shape does not flag a write inside the declared rank, a change spread by quantizing again, or a tensor whose shorter side is below 32 (it lists those), behavior shows a backdoor only when its target leaks to ordinary prompts, and from the trigger output the readers of our blind tests named the trigger's words for at most 2 of 5 backdoors, and 2 of 4. In our Q4_K_M GGUF test shape flagged nothing on all 12 models (the rounding hid the LoRA's rank). inspect gguf was tested on Qwen3.5 with Q4_K_M only.
  • Tested primarily on Apple Silicon: MLX and llama.cpp with Qwen3.5 (0.8B, 4B, 9B), Qwen3-8B, and (for kestrom kv / kv: and kestrom bridge) Gemma 4 E4B; PyTorch with Qwen3.5 0.8B and 9B on MPS and 0.8B on the CPU; and Linux + NVIDIA L4 CUDA (torch 2.14.1+cu130, bitsandbytes 0.50.2) for kestrom ifc, kestrom inspect mirror/disarm (bitsandbytes NF4, FP4, INT8), and kestrom-verify generate torch / compare events / diff on Qwen3.5-0.8B/4B (plus benign DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B mirror scan; kestrom audit invokes diff and inspect mirror and is unit-tested on Linux CI with NumPy nf4, not yet run end-to-end on CUDA). Not tested on Linux/CUDA yet: weight edits (rows, edit), kv/rules/bridge, inspect commands outside mirror/disarm, logits/measure, models whose output layer is tied to the embedding in GGUF. For a tied output layer (Qwen3.5-0.8B), a changed row is also an input: the guarantees hold for the inputs (prompts, teacher-forced sequences) that hold no changed id, and the reports count the others.

Related work

  • Fine-Tuning Integrity (arXiv 2604.04738) proves cryptographically that a deployed model differs from a base only within a declared class of updates. Kestrom's diff checks the same kind of declaration in the clear, by recomputation, when both weights are at hand.
  • Weight diff tools (ckpt, weight-inspect) compare tensors; Kestrom adds the declaration check, reports that rebuild to the same bytes, and output guarantees where the edit allows them.
  • Conditional activation steering (CAST, arXiv 2409.05907), orthogonal Procrustes cross-model alignment (Plato's Key, Hazy Research, 2026), the Antislop backtracking sampler (arXiv 2510.15061), and transformers' no_repeat_ngram_size are the methods behind the in … prompt and add lines, the phrase lines, rows ftpo and the loopguard line; Kestrom adds the range and its check. Astra's edit (rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming) is the form of edit subtract.
  • find, add lines and edit use the logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020), differences of means as directions (CAA, arXiv 2312.06681), ablating and scaling heads (Michel et al., arXiv 1905.10650), MLP neurons as keys and values (Geva et al., arXiv 2012.14913), and rank-1 writes kept off the inputs to preserve (ROME, arXiv 2202.05262; AlphaEdit, arXiv 2410.02355). The combination and the defaults of the neuron and head edits follow the documentation of gguf-neuron-explorer.
  • Smoothie-Qwen also rewrites the output layer to suppress tokens.
  • kestrom inspect compares a fine-tune with its original, as do spectral checks of fine-tunes and LoRA adapters (MIST, arXiv 2605.21146; PEFTGuard, arXiv 2411.17453) and the tracing of rank-one edits (arXiv 2505.20819); Microsoft's scanner (2026) looks for backdoors without the original. What it adds is the reading against the declared recipe: reference fine-tunes retrained from it, and for QLoRA the original quantized again with the setting the weights show.

At decode time, kestrom generate --rules evaluates any in NAME: prompt FILE LAYER conditions (including cross-model probes mapped by kestrom bridge map) on the raw prompt before decoding and passes their 0/1 results into data["values"] alongside each prompt's data (with "steps", into the last step's: earlier steps give their own; values given in data win; allowing "data" to be omitted when the bank reads only those prompt inputs): when an entry uniquely matches (or 2..MAX_MATCH match when MAX_MATCH > 1, composed and prefilled once via an in-memory LRU cache), only the prompt tokens after the shared prefix (with zero knowledge text in the prompt) are decoded on top of that cache, recording event 0 and "kv": KEY (a list when composed); when no entry matches (or more than MAX_MATCH match), no cache is injected and the kv line records no event ("kv": null); where no other line of the rules acts, events=[] and the output is bit-identical to the unchanged model. Because event 0 marks the start of a matched prompt, kestrom-verify compare events checks unmatched prompts up to the first event of another line and covers nothing after position 0 on matched ones. For multi-turn conversations, kestrom kv chat (MODEL BANK_DIR [MAX_TOKENS] [MAX_MATCH] [TURNS.json] [OUT.jsonl] [PROBES.dsl]) evaluates optional PROBES.dsl in ... prompt conditions on each raw turn together with the cumulative steps history through the bank's prev rules, reuses the live KV cache incrementally while the active keys stay unchanged and the chat template remains a strict prefix extension, and swaps/composes/re-prefills only when topics change or history tokens shift. Both kestrom generate and kestrom kv chat refuse a bank whose rules.dsl or cache files are not the ones its manifest.json hashed, or whose model fingerprint differs; the mechanism requires a chat template that places the system turn as a clean prefix before the user turn. kestrom rules run RULES.dsl DATA.json OUT.jsonl runs rules of in, h1, h2, out and set lines as a network of their own, with no model: match, count and number lines read each entry's text by a regex, the other inputs are values given in DATA, and the out lines name classes. A layer may have any number of units. An entry may be a list of steps: the network runs once per step and in NAME: prev UNIT reads whether a unit fired at the step before, so the rules can keep a state (a parity, a mode, what was seen). A set REGISTER: a % b if UNIT line keeps a number along the steps and rewrites it where a unit fires, computed with + - * / // % (a counter, Euclid's algorithm); after one step it is a numeric output, scored against targets. Classes named HEAD/CLASS are answered per head. kestrom rules weigh RULES.dsl DATA.json OUT.dsl rewrites the out lines with coefficients fitted to the labels. run prints how many answers agree with the labels. Use it to try rules on inputs you choose, or to write a small classifier by hand. It edits nothing, so it has no tier; where a rule can be written as plain code, plain code does the same job. Related work Fine-Tuning Integrity (arXiv 2604.04738) proves cryptographically that a deployed model differs from a base only within a declared class of updates. Kestrom's diff checks the same kind of declaration in the clear, by recomputation, when both weights are at hand. Weight diff tools (ckpt, weight-inspect) compare tensors; Kestrom adds the declaration check, reports that rebuild to the same bytes, and output guarantees where the edit allows them.
